paper_title: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Benchmark compression reduces the often prohibitive time and cost of model evaluation by evaluating models on a small benchmark subset that closely matches full-benchmark results. To quantify estimation error, we derive an accurate analytical approximation to the error distribution when estimating full-benchmark scores from a subset, showing that most subsets yield small errors, while a few produce much larger errors, resulting in a long-tailed distribution. This means random sampling alone can achieve surprisingly strong performance with high probability, but remains unstable due to rare large errors. We further show that this instability is inherent to modern foundation models and persists even as more models are evaluated. Based on these findings, we introduce BestRand, a stable and low-cost benchmark compression method that preserves the efficiency of random sampling while substantially reducing its high-error tail. We validate BestRand on 70+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks, and further extend it to VLA evaluation. Compared with competitive methods, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4% on average, while requiring only 51.3% of the construction cost. It further reduces OOD estimation error by 21.8% on average across score-range, model-family, and temporal shifts. Together, our theory provides practical guidance for understanding and predicting the accuracy and reliability of benchmark compression, while BestRand enables stable and accurate compression at low cost. The code and data are publicly available onhttps://github.com/George-Ling3/BestRand.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) on benchmarks can require substantial time and compute (Polo et al., 2024), as these benchmarks often contain many test examples and may also include redundant ones (Zhang et al., 2025b). Benchmark compression reduces this burden by evaluating models on small subset to approximate full-benchmark results (Vivek et al., 2024). Yet the accuracy and reliability of this approximation are not well characterized. To quantify estimation error, we derive an accurate analytical approximation to the error distribution when using subset to estimate full-benchmark scores (Truong et al., 2025). Our theoretical and empirical results show that most subsets yield small errors, while few produce much larger errors, resulting in long-tailed distribution. This means random sampling alone can achieve surprisingly strong performance with high probability (Saranathan et al., 2025), but remains unstable due to rare large errors (Huang et al., 2025b). We further explain this high-probability effectiveness and show that the instability arises from the similarity among LLMs and VLMs and persists even as more models are evaluated. Beyond explaining these phenomena, our theory quantifies the relationship between subset size and estimation error (Zhang et al., 2025a), guiding the balance between evaluation accuracy and cost (Perlitz et al., 2024). Across all theoretical results, numerical experiments consistently agree with our theory. Figure 1 and Appendix provide extensive numerical validation. Motivated by our theory, we introduce BestRand, stable and low-cost benchmark compression method that preserves the efficiency of random sampling while substantially reducing its high-error tail. BestRand generates multiple random subsets and uses few probe models to search for the best candidate. Our theory identifies mechanism by which probe-guided selection can reduce commonshift variability, motivating BestRands design. Experiments demonstrate its improved MAE stability. We validate BestRand on 70+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks, and further extend it 1 Figure 1: Empirical results are consistent with our theory. Bottom: ρ is generally positive; higher ρ theoretically yields longer tails, while ρ and strongly predict empirical MAE P95, which captures long-tail risk. Additional validation is provided in Appendix F. to VLA evaluation. Against competitive methods, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4% on average, while requiring only 51.3% of the construction cost. It further reduces OOD estimation error by 21.8% on average across score-range, model-family, and temporal shifts. Together, our theory provides framework for understanding and guiding benchmark compression, while BestRand turns these insights into stable and low-cost method. We discuss related works in Appendix and summarize our contributions as follows: Theory. We derive an accurate analytical approximation to the error distribution for benchmark compression, explaining why random sampling is effective with high probability yet remains unstable. We further identify inherent similarity among foundation models as primary source of this instability. Extensive numerical experiments are highly consistent with our theory. Method. We propose BestRand, stable and low-cost benchmark compression method that improves random sampling through lightweight probe-guided search, with theoretical support for improved stability. We validate BestRand on 70+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks, as well as VLA evaluation, showing strong accuracy, stability, and OOD generalization at low cost.

sections.title: 3 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate BestRand on 70 text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks, focusing on estimation accuracy and stability. We compare average errors across methods and compression budgets, then examine error distributions and high-error risk, with VLA results reported in the Appendix C. We first introduce the benchmarks, then describe the baselines, evaluation protocol, and metrics. Benchmarks and budgets. Our evaluation spans 70 benchmarks, comprising 44 text, 16 multimodal, and 10 agent benchmarks. These include widely used text benchmarks such as MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), and HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), multimodal benchmarks such as MMMU (Yue et al., 2024), MathVista (Lu et al., 2024), and MME (Fu et al., 2025a), and agent benchmarks such as OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024) and tau-bench (Yao et al., 2024). To compare methods comprehensively across compression levels, we evaluate six retention ratios ranging from 2% to 50%. Details of all benchmarks are provided in Appendix A.2. Baselines and evaluation protocol. We compare against six representative baselines. Random uniformly samples subset and averages its scores. SparseEval (Zhang et al., 2026) uses linear or 6 Figure 3: High-error risk across text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks. Worst-30% entry and worse-than-average entry use Randoms 70th-percentile and mean errors as thresholds, respectively. Whiskers show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. BestRand achieves the lowest risk in all settings. Rand, Zip, Tiny, AP, SE-M, and SE-L denote Random, ZipBench, TinyBenchmarks, Anchor Points, SparseEval MLP, and SparseEval Linear, respectively. Detailed results are shown in Figure 6. MLP predictor to estimate full-benchmark scores from subset scores. Anchor Points, TinyBenchmarks, and ZipBench (Vivek et al., 2024; Polo et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2026) construct item representations and cluster them to select representative subset. All methods use the same model split and item budget. Random and BestRand use 10,000 seeds, while other methods use three. BestRand uses = 5, = 128, = 4, random probe selection, and L2 matching. It probes only the candidate pool and thus incurs lower construction cost. Section 4 further compares four additional baselines. Appendices A.1 and A.3 provide details on the data splits and baselines, respectively. Evaluation metrics. We use mean absolute error (MAE) as our primary metric. We also evaluate ranking fidelity using Spearmans rank correlation coefficient (SP). Since rank correlations are generally strong for leading methods in both our experiments and prior work (Yauney et al., 2026), we focus on MAE in the main results and report detailed SP results in Appendix E, Tables 911. We then compare BestRand with existing methods, showing its high accuracy, low cost, and stability. Main results. As shown in Table 1, Random performs strongly on average. BestRand consistently improves on this baseline, reducing both mean MAE and its variation across all settings. Against three competitive baselines, namely Random, ZipBench, and TinyBenchmarks, BestRand reduces MAE by 16.4% on average, achieving the best overall performance. By probing only candidate pool, BestRand uses just 8.0% of data-dependent baselines construction records at 2% retention and 51.3% on average. BestRand therefore achieves the lowest error at roughly half the construction cost. Beyond average performance, we next compare the stability and high-error risk of all methods. Stability and high-error risk. Figure 2 shows that BestRand concentrates errors near zero and suppresses Randoms upper tail, yielding more stable estimates. Figure 3 quantifies the risk of falling into the high-error region of Randoms long-tailed distribution. We measure the probability that each methods error exceeds Randoms 70th percentile or mean, corresponding to the worst 30% of random subsets and worse-than-average random performance, respectively. Under both thresholds, BestRand achieves the lowest risk across benchmark categories and reduces high-error probability by 50.2% versus three strong baselines. Additional results are reported in Appendix E. Together, these results demonstrate that BestRand enables accurate and stable benchmark compression.

Additional analyses are provided in Appendix C. 7 Figure 4: BestRand ablations at 20% retention. (a) Effects of the number of probe models, the number of candidate subsets, and the candidate-pool size. (b) Performance comparison with more construction models. (c) Effect of probe-model selection. (d) Effect of the matching norm. (1) Effects of Probe Count, Candidate Count, and Pool Multiplier on Performance. We first examine how the probe count p, candidate count m, and pool multiplier affect compression accuracy. As shown in Figure 4(a), more probes improve the reliability of candidate comparison, more candidates increase the chance of finding representative subset, and larger pool provides more accurate reference and greater candidate diversity. Performance improves with all three quantities, but the gains from increasing and quickly diminish. We therefore use = 5, = 128, and = 4 by default. This setting achieves strong accuracy at low construction cost. (2) Does BestRand Remain Competitive as More Construction Models Become Available? Because our main experiments use only five construction models, we next test whether BestRand remains competitive when more models are available. Figure 4(b) shows that BestRand performs best with only few construction models. Learning-based methods improve as they gain more response records, but BestRand remains comparable to the strongest alternatives even with hundreds or thousands of models. Thus, BestRand offers the greatest gains when construction data are limited while retaining competitive accuracy when they are abundant. The low-data setting is also more practical because collecting complete benchmark responses from many models is often costly. (3) Sensitivity to Probe-Model Selection and Matching Norm. We next assess the sensitivity of BestRand to probe selection and matching norm. We compare probes sampled uniformly across the score range, at random, or from its low and high ends. Using two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across benchmarks, Figure 4(c) shows no significant differences except between Uniform and Low, where Uniform performs better. This suggests that probe selection should avoid using only low-scoring models. Figure 4(d) shows similar results for L1, L2, and L, with no significant differences according to the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. BestRand is therefore robust to both choices, and we use random selection with L2 matching by default. (4) Does BestRand Provide Better AccuracyCost Trade-off than Existing Methods? Family OOD uses disjoint model families for construction and testing. Temporal OOD uses older models for construction and newer models for testing. Methods that learn from historical performance records perform worse than Random in every setting, showing that fitting these records can hurt under distribution shifts. In contrast, BestRand achieves the lowest error in all five settings and reduces average OOD error by 21.8% relative to competitive baselines.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this paper, we developed theoretical framework that characterizes the error distribution of benchmark compression and provides principled basis for understanding and predicting its accuracy and reliability. Extensive empirical results closely match our theoretical results. Guided by our theory, we introduced BestRand, which improves the stability of random sampling at low construction cost. Across 70+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks, together with VLA evaluation, BestRand improved accuracy and stability over strong baselines and remained robust to distribution shifts. More broadly, our findings suggest that improving benchmark compression may not require complex selection, but rather understanding when and why simple sampling fails and correcting it at low cost.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: AI assistants were used in this work exclusively for language polishing and code implementation. All research ideas and scientific conclusions are original contributions of the authors. The authors reviewed all LLM-assisted outputs and take full responsibility for the final content of this paper.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: To support reproducibility, we document all key methodological, experimental, and theoretical details. Section 2 presents the complete formulation and procedure of BestRand. Sections 3 and 4 specify the evaluation protocol, metrics, default settings, ablations, construction cost, and OOD evaluation. Appendix gives the model splits, benchmark sources and metrics, baseline details, and hyperparameters. Appendices and report detailed results and describe the protocols for the VLA, multi-metric, and data-only experiments. Appendix contains the full proofs, derivations, assumption checks, and numerical validation. We will make all code and data publicly available.

(2025a). 21 A.3 DETAILS OF BASELINES CONSIDERED We group the baselines by whether benchmark construction uses historical model responses. Response-based methods use these records to identify representative items and, when needed, learn how to estimate full-benchmark scores from selected-item responses. Random and the data-only methods use no historical performance records and are collectively termed response-free methods. Response-based baselines differ in their item representations and score estimators. SparseEval (Zhang et al., 2026) represents each item by its response vector across construction models. Starting from clustered or random subset, it iteratively replaces items to reduce full-score prediction error on the construction models. linear model or MLP then maps new models selected-item responses to its estimated full score. Anchor Points (Vivek et al., 2024) derives item similarities from correlations between response patterns and applies k-medoids clustering. It selects each cluster medoid and estimates performance using cluster-size-weighted average of the selected-item scores. TinyBenchmarks (Polo et al., 2024) fits an item response theory model to learn item difficulty and discrimination, clusters the resulting item representations, and selects one representative per cluster. For new model, it infers ability from the selected responses and predicts performance on unobserved items. We use its gp-IRT estimator, which combines these predictions with the weighted observed-item score. ZipBench (Huang et al., 2026) is designed for settings with limited construction budgets. It constructs synthetic response records by majority voting within group of construction models and retains records spanning the observed performance range. It then fits an item response theory model to the augmented records, clusters the learned item representations, and estimates the full score using cluster-size-weighted average of the selected-item scores. Among the response-free baselines, Random uniformly samples subset of items, whereas the four data-only methods select subsets using prompt-derived representations. All five methods estimate each models full-benchmark score by averaging its scores on the selected items. Facility Location, MIS, and Coverage use Sentence-BERT embeddings (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019), whereas Agreement uses multilingual BERT representations (Devlin et al., 2019). Facility Location (Yao et al., 2026) greedily selects items that maximize semantic coverage, ensuring that each benchmark item is close to selected item. MIS (Kjorvezir et al., 2026) connects semantically similar prompts in graph and greedily selects an independent set to reduce redundancy. Agreement (Purificato et al., 2026) applies an eight-head attention module to the BERT representations, ranks prompts by the variance of their attention weights, and retains those with the greatest disagreement. Coverage (Purificato et al., 2026) begins with random prompt and repeatedly selects the prompt farthest from the most recently chosen one, encouraging coverage of distinct regions in the embedding space. A.4 IMPLEMENTATION AND HYPERPARAMETERS Main experiment. BestRand uses five probe models, 128 candidate subsets, pool multiplier of four, and L2 matching. We evaluate Random and BestRand over 10,000 trials to obtain stable estimates. We evaluate other baselines with three seeds to obtain reliable results. Anchor Points uses FasterPAM for k-medoids clustering. TinyBenchmarks and ZipBench use multidimensional two-parameter logistic IRT models with 10 and 5 dimensions, respectively. Both IRT models are trained for 2,000 epochs with an initial learning rate of 0.1 and decay factor of 0.9999. ZipBench adds six synthetic response profiles. SparseEval performs 10 subset-refinement rounds and trains each proxy for 2,000 epochs. Its MLP has hidden widths of 128, 64, and 32 with dropout 0.1. Both the linear and MLP variants use learning rate of 5 104 and train the final predictor for up to 20,000 epochs, with early stopping checked every 500 epochs using patience of 30. Data-only experiment. We evaluate data-only methods in Section 4 and Appendix C.3 as response-free baselines. We evaluate the four methods at 20% retention on the 12 text benchmarks used in the cost analysis. The primary setting uses 384-dimensional Sentence-BERT representations, while RoBERTa, RoBERTas last-layer representation, and Longformer are used only for embedding sensitivity. Agreement uses bert-base-multilingual-uncased, maximum sequence length of 64, eight attention heads, and batch size of 32. MIS estimates its similarity threshold from 10,000 randomly sampled prompt pairs and searches percentiles 80 through 100 until the item budget can be met. Facility Location chooses its neighborhood scale from {0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, 100} by three-fold validation based only on geometric coverage. 22 Table 5: Comparison of the construction information required by BestRand and 15 diverse baselines. Among response-based methods, BestRand has lower information requirements because it uses scores from only subset of items, reducing construction cost while retaining strong empirical performance. In Section 4, we evaluate OOD generalization at 20% retention under scorerange, model-family, and temporal shifts. For score-range OOD, we rank models by their fullbenchmark scores, randomly sample construction models from the lowest, highest, or middle 75%, and reserve the complementary 25% for testing. Full scores are used only to define the OOD splits, and no test-model responses are used for item selection or estimator fitting. Model-family OOD uses disjoint families for construction and testing, while temporal OOD uses only models released earlier than every test model for construction. We use five splits with different random seeds for each shift setting to reduce sensitivity to any single model split. For each split, we evaluate Random and BestRand with 100 seeds and all other baselines with three seeds. We average MAE over seeds and splits within each benchmark, then report the mean and standard deviation across benchmarks. Additional baseline experiment. In Appendix E.3, we evaluate five additional baselines on 12 benchmarks using three random seeds for each stochastic method and single run for the deterministic DatBench. SubLIME uses BERT representations and rank correlation predictor to select from 1,000 candidate subsets after transport filtering. MINCE estimates score drift from 10,000 Monte Carlo subsets per retention ratio. EssenceBench uses BGE-M3 representations, redundancy thresholds of 0.9, three genetic search rounds, and regularized predictor with 25 spline terms. FlashEval retains the top 100,000 of three million candidates according to Kendalls τb. DatBench ranks binary items by point-biserial correlation and uses Pearson correlation for nonbinary scores. All methods use identical data splits and item budgets, and test responses are used only for final evaluation. Construction information requirements. Among response-based methods, BestRand has relatively low information requirements because its probe models score only candidate pool rather than the full benchmark. This partial coverage reduces the required construction data and construction cost.

sections.content: D.1 LIMITATIONS OF BESTRAND BestRand provides an efficient approximation to full evaluation, but several limitations remain. Nonzero estimation error. Although BestRand outperforms many existing benchmark compression methods at lower construction cost, it cannot guarantee zero estimation error. This is common limitation of benchmark compression, but the compression ratio can be adjusted to balance evaluation efficiency and reliability. BestRand is most useful for rapid model iteration and comparison, but compressed benchmarks cannot fully replace comprehensive evaluation. We therefore recommend reporting full-benchmark results for final evaluations when feasible. Probe inference cost. BestRand still requires probe models to run full inference on some benchmark items, so its construction cost is not zero. However, this cost is small in practice and brings clear accuracy gains. BestRand substantially outperforms data-only methods that use no model responses. Moreover, only few probe models are needed, and they score only the candidate pool, which can be much smaller than the full benchmark at low retention ratios. BestRand therefore achieves better accuracy at lower construction cost than existing response-based methods. D.2 BROADER IMPACT OF BESTRAND BestRand provides stable, accurate, and low-cost benchmark compression, reducing evaluation costs while preserving reliable results. Its efficient construction process also keeps the cost of creating compressed benchmarks low. Together, these benefits can reduce compute and energy use, lower associated carbon emissions, and support faster experimental iteration. By making reliable evaluation more affordable, BestRand can also lower barriers for smaller laboratories and researchers with limited computing resources, enabling broader participation in model development and evaluation. All benchmark compression experiments can run on single GPU. BestRands subset selection requires only CPU and completes in under 0.1 seconds with parallel execution. sections.title: G RELATED WORK
sections.content: G.1 LLM, VLM, AND VLA BENCHMARKS Benchmarks for LLMs, VLMs, and VLAs evaluate broad range of capabilities across text, multimodal, and interactive tasks (Hendrycks et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2024; Dauner et al., 2024; Ling et al., 2026a; Zhong et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Examples include LongBench v2, MMMU, and Bench2Drive (Bai et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2024; Jia et al., 2024). Evaluating modern foundation models can be expensive even for individual items, particularly when models process long contexts, generate extended reasoning chains, or perform repeated inference during interaction with an environment (Huang et al., 2025b; Bai et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2024). This cost accumulates across benchmarks containing hundreds to tens of thousands of evaluation items (Polo et al., 2024; Perlitz et al., 2024). Many benchmarks also contain redundancy, as different items can provide overlapping information about model capabilities (Zhang et al., 2025b; Vivek et al., 2024). Prior studies show that small subsets can closely approximate full-benchmark scores or preserve model rankings, suggesting that much of the information needed for aggregate evaluation can be retained with fewer items (Vivek et al., 2024; Polo et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025b; Saranathan et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026). BestRand exploits this redundancy to reduce evaluation cost across these settings while improving the accuracy and stability of evaluation on compact subsets. G.2 LOW-COST DEEP LEARNING Improving efficiency and reducing training and inference costs have long been central goals in deep learning, with methods operating on both models and data (Wan et al., 2023). On the model side, pruning and quantization improve inference efficiency (Han et al., 2015; Frantar & Alistarh, 2023; Xiao et al., 2023), while parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the resources required to adapt pretrained models (Houlsby et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2021). On the data side, coreset selection and data pruning retain informative training examples (Mirzasoleiman et al., 2020; Paul et al., 2021), while dataset condensation synthesizes compact training sets that approximate the learning signal of larger datasets (Zhao et al., 2020; Cazenavette et al., 2022). BestRand applies this data-efficiency perspective to model evaluation by selecting reusable subset of existing test items that closely preserves full-benchmark results at low construction cost. By reducing the number of evaluated items, BestRand complements methods that reduce the cost of processing each item. G.3 BENCHMARK COMPRESSION METHODS Benchmark compression reduces the number of evaluated items while preserving full-benchmark scores or model rankings. (Ling et al., 2026b; Lin et al., 2026) For constructing reusable subsets, useful distinction is whether methods use historical item-level model responses. Methods without such records use random sampling or select representative items through prompt embeddings and other content-derived features, typically using clustering or diversity-based selection (Song et al., 2025a; Bean et al., 2025). Response-based methods instead exploit evaluation results from previously tested models to identify informative items through response-pattern clustering, item response modeling, or learned score prediction (Vivek et al., 2024; Polo et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026). Many such methods rely on large collections of model evaluations, making subset construction expensive for new benchmarks without public evaluation logs (Bean et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026). Efforts to reduce this dependence include learning from small anchor sets, augmenting observed responses with synthetic records, and calibrating random subset sizes using few models (Saranathan et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Das et al., 2026). Beyond method development, prior analyses examine benchmark redundancy (Zhang et al., 2025b; Sha & Zhao, 2026) and the statistical reliability of model comparisons (Miller, 2024; Heineman et al., 2025). Studies of compressed evaluation further highlight sensitivity to calibration data and model shifts, the limitations of very small subsets, and the competitiveness of random sampling (Zhang et al., 2025a; Yauney et al., 2026). Our theory complements these perspectives by characterizing the distribution of compression errors, explaining persistent high-error risk and providing principled basis for reducing it. BestRand offers improved accuracy and stability over random sampling with lower construction cost than methods that rely on extensive historical evaluation records. Detailed descriptions of the baselines considered in our experiments are provided in Appendix A.3.

sections.title: H THE NOVELTY AND CONTRIBUTION OF BESTRAND
sections.content: H.1 NOVELTY OF BESTRAND Our novelty follows clear progression. We first derive theoretical characterization of benchmark compression and explain its behavior, then use these insights to improve its reliability and stability. An accurate characterization of the error distribution in benchmark compression. We derive an accurate analytical approximation to the MAE distribution when benchmark subset is used to estimate full-benchmark scores. This distribution-level view goes beyond average error and ranking fidelity by describing both typical outcomes and high-error outcomes. It therefore provides principled basis for understanding the accuracy and reliability of benchmark compression. Numerical results across LLM, VLM, and VLA benchmarks closely match the predicted distributions. An explanation of why random sampling is almost enough. Our analysis shows that the MAE distribution has dominant low-error region. As the number of evaluated models grows, its mode approaches the lower endpoint of the limiting distribution at universal rate. Together with the observed concentration around this region, this result explains why random sampling produces accurate compressed benchmarks with high probability and is often strong baseline. The locations of the empirical modes are consistent with the theoretical prediction. An explanation of the persistent instability of random sampling. We identify the common shift, caused by subset being easier or harder than the full benchmark, as key source of the upper error tail. Its scale grows with behavioral correlation across models and remains positive as model count grows under positive correlation. Thus, evaluating more models cannot average away shared errors. This persistent instability reflects correlated behavior among foundation models, consistent with relationships among model correlation, common-shift scale, and high-error risk. theoretically grounded, stable, and low-cost method. This analysis motivates BestRand. We decompose the common shift into probe-explained and residual components. BestRand draws multiple random subsets and selects the one whose mean probe scores best match pool reference to control the explained component. Under our selection model, theory guarantees that the commonshift variance converges to value strictly below that of random sampling as the probe imbalance vanishes, thereby improving stability. Experiments consistently confirm this theoretical prediction. H.2 CONTRIBUTIONS OF BESTRAND Together, these theoretical insights and methodological advances yield three main contributions. theoretical framework for benchmark compression. We derive exact sampling moments and an accurate analytical approximation to the MAE distribution. The framework connects compression error and high-error risk to the subset size, item difficulty variation, and model correlation. The theory further shows that matching probe-model scores can reduce common-shift variance. Extensive numerical validation shows that the predicted distributions, modes, and tail-related quantities closely match empirical measurements, supporting both the validity and practical value of the theory. stable and low-cost compression method. We introduce BestRand, which uses few probe models to select from random subsets. These probe models evaluate only small subset of benchmark items rather than the full benchmark, so construction cost is low. Our theory shows that sufficiently accurate probe matching gives BestRand lower common-shift variance than Random and thus greater stability. Experiments consistently confirm this stability gain. Extensive empirical validation and strong results. We evaluate BestRand on 70 text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks across various retention ratios, and further extend it to VLA evaluation. The empirical error distributions closely match our theoretical analysis, and BestRand consistently suppresses the high-error region predicted by the theory. It improves estimation accuracy at low construction cost while maintaining strong ranking fidelity. These gains remain consistent under score-range, model-family, and temporal shifts, supporting its robustness to unseen target models.
